claims.source: The inheritance of the inducible heterochromatic domain depends on the read-write capability of Clr4 and can be readily observed in cells in which the anti-silencing factor epe1+, encoding a Jmjc family demethylase member, has been deleted (Trewick et al., 2007; Bao et al., 2019; Sorida et al., 2019; Ragunathan et al., 2015; Audergon et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Mutation or deletion of the chromodomain of Clr4 specifically disrupts epigenetic inheritance without any effect on heterochromatin establishment.
claims.source: Mutation or deletion of the chromodomain of Clr4, required for efficient read-write, specifically disrupt epigenetic inheritance without any effect on heterochromatin establishment (Ragunathan et al., 2015; Audergon et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In wild-type epe1+ cells, epigenetic inheritance of heterochromatin requires input from specific DNA sequences or a locally generated siRNA amplification loop.
claims.source: In wild-type epe1+ cells, in addition to the read-write mechanism, epigenetic inheritance of heterochromatin requires input from specific DNA sequences or a locally generated siRNA amplification loop (Wang and Moazed, 2017; Yu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The genetic screen identified mutations in several pathways, including known heterochromatin associated factors, components of the DNA replication machinery, and three subunits of an RNA processing complex.
claims.source: Our screen identified mutations in several pathways, including mutations in known heterochromatin associated factors, components of the DNA replication machinery, and in three subunits of an RNA processing complex, composed of Rix1, Crb3, Grc3, Mdn1, Las1 and Ipi1 (Castle et al., 2012; Schillewaert et al., 2012; Castle et al., 2013; Gasse et al., 2015; Fromm et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen, supported by whole genome sequencing data presented in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The rixosome complex is conserved from yeast to human.
claims.source: This complex, which we propose to name the 'rixosome', is conserved from yeast to human
claims.evidence: This is supported by the list of human orthologs shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The rixosome has well-characterized essential functions in ribosomal RNA (rRNA) processing.
claims.source: This complex, which we propose to name the 'rixosome', is conserved from yeast to human, has well-characterized essential functions in ribosomal RNA (rRNA) processing
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Castle et al., 2012; Schillewaert et al., 2012; Castle et al., 2013; Gasse et al., 2015; Fromm et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The rixosome has been previously shown to localize to heterochromatin in a Swi6-dependent manner.
claims.source: has been previously shown to localize to heterochromatin in a Swi6-dependent manner (Kitano et al., 2011; Iglesias et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The rixosome targets heterochromatic RNAs for degradation through the conserved 5'−3' exoribonuclease pathway.
claims.source: We show that the rixosome targets heterochromatic RNAs for degradation through the conserved 5'−3' exoribonuclease pathway to clear a path for Clr4-mediated read-write.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental data, including RT-qPCR (Figure 5B, C), small RNA northern blots (Figure 5G, H), and dhp1-1 mutant phenotypes (Figure 4A, B).

claims.claim: The screen identified 83 apparent emd mutants from 80,000 colonies screened.
claims.source: We screened 80,000 colonies and obtained 83 apparent emd mutants
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of the screening results, also shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: About half of the emd mutants showed single-locus segregation patterns in random spore analysis.
claims.source: About half of these mutants showed single-locus segregation patterns in random spore analysis when backcrossed to the original reporter strain.
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of the genetic analysis results.

claims.claim: Out of 40 emd mutants, 30 yielded high confidence single nucleotide variants in coding regions of the genome.
claims.source: Out of the 40 emd mutants, 30 yielded high confidence single nucleotide variants in coding regions of the genome (variants present in >90% of the mutant spore pool)
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of the whole genome sequencing results.

claims.claim: The identified mutations mapped to 19 genes, most of which encode subunits of one of five complexes.
claims.source: The identified mutations mapped to 19 genes, most of which encode subunits of one of five complexes (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of the sequencing analysis results, with data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The screen identified four mutations in three genes encoding subunits of the rixosome: crb3, grc3 and mdn1.
claims.source: we identified four mutations in three genes – crb3, grc3 and mdn1 – coding for subunits of an essential ribosome biogenesis complex that we refer to as the rixosome (Figure 1D)
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of the screening results, with data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The rixosome contains six unique subunits: three structural subunits (Crb3, Rix1 and Ipi1) and three catalytic subunits (Las1, Grc3 and Mdn1).
claims.source: The rixosome contains six unique subunits – three structural subunits Crb3, Rix1 and Ipi1, which form the core of the complex, and three catalytic subunits – the endonuclease Las1, the polynucleotide kinase Grc3 and the AAA-type ATPase Mdn1, which are involved in the processing of ribosomal RNA precursors (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Fromm et al., 2017; Gasse et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: All subunits of the rixosome are essential for viability and are conserved from yeast to mammals, including humans.
claims.source: All subunits are essential for viability and are conserved from yeast to mammals, including humans (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A listing human orthologs.

claims.claim: Three de novo constructed strains carrying rixosome mutations reproduced the mutant phenotypes in plating assays.
claims.source: We validated three of the mutations by reconstituting them de novo in the original reporter strain. All de novo constructed strains reproduced the mutant phenotypes in plating assays on low adenine medium in the presence and absence of tetracycline (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of validation experiments, with data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: In the absence of tetracycline, the rixosome mutants showed similar levels of H3K9me2 as the wild-type.
claims.source: In the absence of tetracycline, the rixosome mutants showed similar levels of H3K9me2 as the wild-type, which is consistent with the lack of silencing defects under the establishment conditions (Figure 2C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: In tetracycline treated cultures, the levels of H3K9me2 were drastically reduced in the rixosome mutants, but not in the wild-type.
claims.source: By contrast, in the tetracycline treated cultures, the levels of H3K9me2 were drastically reduced in the mutants, but not in the wild-type, indicating that loss of silencing of the 10xtetO-ade6+ reporter under the maintenance conditions resulted from loss of the underlying heterochromatic domain (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The crb3-D198N mutation has little or no effect on the establishment of heterochromatin at endogenous domains.
claims.source: These results indicate that the crb3-D198N mutation has little or no effect on the establishment of heterochromatin at endogenous domains, consistent with the phenotype at the ectopic reporter.
claims.evidence: This is supported by silencing assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In ago1Δ cells, H3K9me2 and me3 enrichment was reduced to background levels by the crb3-D198N mutation.
claims.source: By contrast, in ago1Δ cells, where establishment is abolished, H3K9me2 and me3 enrichment was reduced to background levels by the crb3-D198N mutation (Figure 2F,G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claims.claim: While the establishment of RNAi-dependent H3K9me and silencing at endogenous pericentromeric repeats does not require the rixosome, the epigenetic maintenance of H3K9me at these regions is completely rixosome-dependent.
claims.source: These results show that while the establishment of RNAi-dependent H3K9me and silencing at endogenous pericentromeric repeats does not require the rixosome, the epigenetic maintenance of H3K9me at these regions is completely rixosome-dependent.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP data in Figure 2F and 2G, comparing ago1+ and ago1Δ cells.

claims.claim: The grc3-V70M mutation does not cause rRNA processing defects.
claims.source: By contrast, no rRNA precursors accumulated in the grc3-V70M mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), which we therefore conclude is a separation-of-function allele best suited for further analysis of rixosome function in heterochromatin formation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by rRNA processing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The Crb3-TAP purification from wild-type cells pulled down the core subunits reported previously to be part of the rixosome.
claims.source: The Crb3-TAP purification from wild-type cells pulled down the core subunits reported previously to be part of the rixosome (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by TMT-MS data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The Crb3-TAP purification from wild-type cells recovered the heterochromatin-associated protein Swi6.
claims.source: Importantly, we also recovered the heterochromatin-associated protein Swi6, which was previously shown to associate with the rixosome in an H3K9me-independent manner (Iglesias et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TMT-MS data shown in Figure 3B and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: When Crb3-TAP was purified from cells carrying the grc3-V70M mutation, the levels of Swi6 copurifying with the mutant complex were dramatically reduced.
claims.source: By contrast, when we purified Crb3-TAP from cells carrying the grc3-V70M mutation, the levels of Swi6 copurifying with the mutant complex were dramatically reduced, but the mutation had little or no effect on the overall integrity of the rixosome and its other interactions (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TMT-MS data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Neither the crb3-D198N, nor the grc3-V70M mutations had any effect on the total levels of Swi6 in the cell.
claims.source: Furthermore, neither the crb3-D198N, nor the grc3-V70M mutations had any effect on the total levels of Swi6 in the cell, ruling out that the loss of association of the rixosome with Swi6 could be an indirect effect of reduced Swi6 expression or stability (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The Grc3-V70M mutation specifically disrupts the association of the rixosome complex with Swi6.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that the Grc3-V70M mutation specifically disrupts the association of the rixosome complex with Swi6 and further support a specific role for the complex in heterochromatin maintenance, independent of its essential function in ribosome biogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TMT-MS and western blot data in Figure 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: The Grc3-V70M mutation is located in the unstructured N-terminus of Grc3 within a VxVxV sequence motif, a variant of the consensus PxVxL motif of proteins which interact directly with the chromoshadow domain of HP1 proteins.
claims.source: The Grc3-V70M mutation is located in the unstructured N-terminus of Grc3 within a VxVxV sequence motif, a variant of the consensus PxVxL motif of proteins, which interact directly with the chromoshadow domain of HP1 proteins (Figure 3D; Thiru et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the domain diagram in Figure 3D and citation to previous work on HP1 interaction motifs.

claims.claim: Swi6 likely interacts directly with the N-terminus of Grc3 via its chromoshadow domain.
claims.source: Therefore, Swi6 likely interacts directly with the N-terminus of Grc3 via its chromoshadow domain.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the location of the mutation in a known HP1-binding motif and the loss of Swi6 interaction in the mutant.

claims.claim: Crb3-TAP co-localized with H3K9me2-containing heterochromatic domains.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3E,F and G, Crb3-TAP co-localized with H3K9me2-containing heterochromatic domains.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E, F, and G.

claims.claim: Crb3-TAP localized to the clusters of tRNA genes concentrated at the boundaries of the centromeres and to the inverted repeat regions, IR-L and IR-R, of the mat locus.
claims.source: In addition, Crb3-TAP localized to the clusters of tRNA genes concentrated at the boundaries of the centromeres and to the inverted repeat regions, IR-L and IR-R, of the mat locus (Figure 3E,F), which carry B-box sites and recruit TFIIIC (Noma et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3E and F, with citation to previous work on TFIIIC recruitment.

claims.claim: In the grc3-V70M mutant, heterochromatin localization of Crb3-TAP was reduced to background levels.
claims.source: By contrast, in the grc3-V70M mutant, heterochromatin localization of Crb3-TAP was reduced to background levels (Figure 3E,F and G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E, F, G, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The grc3-V70M mutation did not affect the localization of Crb3-TAP to the boundaries of the centromeres or the mating type locus.
claims.source: The grc3-V70M mutation did not affect the localization of Crb3-TAP to the boundaries of the centromeres or the mating type locus, indicating that the recruitment of the rixosome to these regions is independent of its ability to interact with Swi6 (Figure 3E,F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claims.claim: Crb3-TAP localized to the ectopically induced domain of H3K9 methylation at the tetO-ade6+ reporter and this localization was abolished in grc3-V70M cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, Crb3-TAP localized to the ectopically induced domain of H3K9 methylation at the tetO-ade6+ reporter and this localization was abolished in grc3-V70M cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), demonstrating that heterochromatin formation was sufficient for rixosome recruitment.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Crb3-TAP was not enriched at the ribosomal DNA loci on chromosome III (25S and 18S rRNA) or the subtelomeric tel1R and tel2L regions in wild-type cells, despite the presence of H3K9me2.
claims.source: Finally, Crb3-TAP was not enriched at the ribosomal DNA loci on chromosome III (25S and 18S rRNA) or the subtelomeric tel1R and tel2L regions in wild-type cells, despite the presence of H3K9me2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: The rixosome showed enrichment at a number of euchromatic loci, which did not contain H3K9me2 and were not affected by the grc3-V70M mutant.
claims.source: In addition to heterochromatic regions, the rixosome showed enrichment at a number of euchromatic loci, which did not contain H3K9me2 and were not affected by the grc3-V70M mutant (Figure 3E,F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E), including protein coding, tRNA and 5S rRNA genes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3E, F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: The grc3-V70M mutation did not affect the levels of H3K9me2 at various heterochromatic loci.
claims.source: Consistent with unperturbed establishment of native heterochromatin in grc3-V70M mutant cells (Figure 1D, Figure 2B), the mutation did not affect the levels of H3K9me2 at various heterochromatic loci (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: The dhp1-1 allele had no effect on silencing of the 10xtetO-ade6+ gene under establishment conditions, but abolished silencing under maintenance conditions.
claims.source: Under establishment conditions, in the absence of tetracycline, the dhp1-1 allele had no effect on silencing of the 10xtetO-ade6+ gene, but abolished silencing under maintenance conditions, in the presence of tetracycline, closely phenocopying the rixosome mutants (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silencing assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: H3K9me2 was lost in dhp1-1 cells in the presence of tetracycline but not in its absence.
claims.source: Consistent with the silencing results, chromatin immunoprecipitation showed that H3K9me2 was lost in dhp1-1 cells, in the presence of tetracycline but not in its absence (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: 5'−3' mediated RNA degradation by Dhp1, rather than 3'−5' mediated RNA degradation by the exosome, is the key event downstream of the rixosome required for epigenetic inheritance.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that 5'−3' mediated RNA degradation by Dhp1, rather than 3'−5' mediated RNA degradation by the exosome, is the key event downstream of the rixosome required for epigenetic inheritance.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the phenotypes of dhp1-1 and dis3-54 mutants (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Expression of wild-type Grc3 largely restored the maintenance defect of the grc3-G409E mutant cells.
claims.source: Expression of wild-type Grc3 largely restored the maintenance defect of the grc3-G409E mutant cells (Figure 4C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silencing assay data shown in Figure 4C and quantification in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Expression of catalytically dead Grc3-K252A, S253A did not rescue the maintenance defect of grc3-G409E mutant cells.
claims.source: By contrast, expression of catalytically dead Grc3-K252A, S253A did not rescue the maintenance defect (Figure 4C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silencing assay data shown in Figure 4C and quantification in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The kinase activity of Grc3, which prepares RNA substrates for 5'−3' exonucleolytic degradation by Dhp1, is essential for epigenetic inheritance of heterochromatin.
claims.source: These observations demonstrate that the kinase activity of Grc3, which prepares RNA substrates for 5'−3' exonucleolytic degradation by Dhp1, is essential for epigenetic inheritance of heterochromatin.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: The caf1Δ grc3-V70M double mutant showed a marked accumulation of gfp transcripts relative to caf1Δ alone.
claims.source: By contrast, the caf1Δ grc3-V70M double mutant showed a marked accumulation of gfp transcripts relative to caf1Δ alone (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: The increase in RNA levels in the caf1Δ grc3-V70M double mutant was not accompanied by a significant increase in RNA Pol II occupancy.
claims.source: The increase in RNA levels in the double mutant was not accompanied by a small increase in RNA Pol II occupancy (Figure 5D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claims.claim: Even under strong establishment conditions, some RNA is transcribed from the 10xtetO-ura4+-gfp locus and is targeted for degradation by the rixosome and Ccr4-Not complex.
claims.source: We conclude that even under strong establishment conditions, in which the 10xtetO-ura4+-gfp reporter is strongly silenced at the phenotypic level, some RNA is transcribed from the locus and is targeted for degradation by the rixosome and Ccr4-Not complex, and that degradation of such 'toxic' RNA by heterochromatin-associated rixosome is required for epigenetic inheritance of H3K9me.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RT-qPCR and ChIP data in Figure 5B-E.

claims.claim: Both grc3-V70M and dhp1-1 mutations caused a marked increase in siRNAs accumulation from pericentromeric dg repeats.
claims.source: We assessed the levels of siRNA generated from the pericentromeric dg repeats in wild-type, grc3-V70M, and dhp1-1 cells by northern blotting and, consistent with the above hypothesis, found that both mutations caused a marked increase in siRNAs accumulation (Figure 5G, lanes 1–3 and H; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by small RNA northern blot data shown in Figure 5G and quantification in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The grc3-V70M dhp1-1 double mutant had siRNA levels comparable to those of each of the single mutants.
claims.source: Moreover, the grc3-V70M dhp1-1 double mutant had siRNA levels comparable to those of each of the single mutants, suggesting that the rixosome and the exonuclease Dhp1 act in the same pathway (Figure 5G, lane 4, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by small RNA northern blot data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claims.claim: dg siRNA levels were similar between swi6Δ grc3+ and swi6Δ grc3-V70M cells, indicating that the ability of the rixosome pathway to compete with RNAi required its Swi6-mediated recruitment.
claims.source: Consistent with the requirement for Swi6 in recruitment of the rixosome to heterochromatin (Iglesias et al., 2020), dg siRNA levels were similar between swi6Δ grc3+ and swi6Δ grc3-V70M cells, indicating that the ability of the rixosome pathway to compete with RNAi required its Swi6-mediated recruitment (Figure 5G, lanes 5 and 6, and H; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by small RNA northern blot data shown in Figure 5G and quantification in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The increased accumulation of pericentromeric dg siRNAs in the mutant cells was accompanied by only a modest increase in full-length dg transcripts.
claims.source: The increased accumulation of pericentromeric dg siRNAs in the above mutant cells was accompanied by only a modest increase in full-length dg transcripts (Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) occupancy at the dg repeats was only weakly affected by the mutations.
claims.source: Finally, RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) occupancy at the dg repeats was only weakly affected (Figure 5J), suggesting that the mutations did not affect the levels of transcription from the repeats.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 5J.

claims.claim: Heterochromatin-associated rixosome cleaves and phosphorylates target RNAs so that they become substrates for degradation by the Dhp1 exonuclease.
claims.source: We therefore conclude that heterochromatin-associated rixosome cleaves and phosphorylates target RNAs so that they become substrates for degradation by the Dhp1 exonuclease.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on RNA accumulation, siRNA levels, and the requirement for Grc3 kinase activity.

claims.claim: The grc3-V70M and dhp1-1 mutant cells displayed a modest reduction in H3K9me3 levels at heterochromatic domains where the rixosome was enriched.
claims.source: While the pattern or levels of H3K9me2 were generally not perturbed in grc3-V70M and dhp1-1 mutants relative to wild-type cells, the mutant cells displayed a modest reduction in H3K9me3 levels. This reduction only occurred at heterochromatic domains where the rixosome was enriched: the mat locus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B), the pericentromeric repeats of cen1, cen2 and cen3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,C,D) and the 10xtetO-ade6+ reporter under establishment conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D.

claims.claim: The L(BglII):ade6+ transgene became fully derepressed in clr4-W31G cells.
claims.source: As expected, the L(BglII):ade6+ transgene became fully derepressed in clr4-W31G cells, indicating that Clr4 read-write was essential for the spread of silencing away from the cenH nucleation region (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silencing assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Both grc3-V70M and dhp1-1 mutants abolished the silencing of the L(BglII):ade6+ transgene.
claims.source: Both mutants abolished the silencing of the ade6+ transgene, in a manner similar to the clr4-W31G mutant, suggesting that the rixosome and Dhp1 were required for the spread of silencing into the transgene (Figure 6C,D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silencing assay data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claims.claim: Analysis of RNA levels using qRT-PCR showed strong accumulation of ade6+ RNA in the grc3-V70M and dhp1-1 mutant cells relative to wild-type cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the colony color assays, analysis of RNA levels using qRT-PCR showed strong accumulation of ade6+ RNA in the grc3-V70M and dhp1-1 mutant cells relative to wild-type cells, to an equal or greater extent as that observed in clr4-W31G and clr4Δ cells, indicating that L(BglII):ade6+ transgene silencing was completely rixosome- and Dhp1-dependent (Figure 6E, primer pair 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Silencing of the mat2P gene, which is H3K9me-independent, was not affected by grc3-V70M, dhp1-1, or clr4 mutations.
claims.source: As expected, silencing of the mat2P gene, which is H3K9me-independent (Hansen et al., 2011), was not affected by any of the above mutations (Figure 6E, primer pair 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6E and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: grc3-V70M, dhp1-1, and clr4 mutations did not significantly affect RNA Pol II occupancy at the cenH region and the ade6+ transgene.
claims.source: Moreover, ChIP-qPCR experiments showed that grc3-V70M, dhp1-1, and clr4 mutations (clr4-W31G and clr4Δ) did not significantly affect RNA Pol II occupancy at the cenH region and the ade6+ transgene (Figure 6F), suggesting that silencing occurred primarily at the level of RNA degradation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: The loss of L(BglII):ade6+ transgene silencing in grc3-V70M and dhp1-1 cells was accompanied by impaired spreading of H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 from the cenH region into the ade6+ transgene and leftward into the IR-L boundary.
claims.source: The loss of L(BglII):ade6+ transgene silencing in grc3-V70M and dhp1-1 cells was accompanied by impaired spreading of H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 from the cenH region into the ade6+ transgene and leftward into the IR-L boundary, while spreading into the mat2P gene occurred with similar efficiency in mutant and wild-type cells (Figure 6G and H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claims.claim: When the ade6+ reporter was absent, the grc3-V70M and dhp1-1 mutations had little or no effect on the spreading of H3K9me into the native IR-L region.
claims.source: Moreover, ChIP-seq experiments showed that when the ade6+ reporter was absent, the grc3-V70M and dhp1-1 mutations had little or no effect on the spreading of H3K9me into the native IR-L region, supporting the idea that the rixosome was required for spreading of H3K9me across the transcriptionally active ade6+ transgene (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: In clr4-W31G cells, the levels of H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 were strongly reduced and did not spread outside the cenH region.
claims.source: Consistent with previous results (Zhang et al., 2008), in clr4-W31G cells, the levels of H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 were strongly reduced and did not spread outside the cenH region (Figure 6G and H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6G and H, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The rixosome plays an essential role in spreading of H3K9me and silencing over a transcription unit that is inserted distal to a heterochromatin nucleation center.
claims.source: These results uncover an essential role for the rixosome in spreading of H3K9me and silencing over a transcription unit that is inserted distal to a heterochromatin nucleation center.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on the L(BglII):ade6+ transgene in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The rixosome is recruited to heterochromatin by the HP1 protein, Swi6, to promote the degradation of RNAs transcribed by RNA pol II within heterochromatic domains.
claims.source: The rixosome is recruited to heterochromatin by the HP1 protein, Swi6, to promote the degradation of RNAs transcribed by RNA pol II within heterochromatic domains.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on Swi6 interaction (Figure 3), localization (Figure 3), and RNA degradation (Figure 5).

claims.claim: The conservation of all rixosome subunits from yeast to human raises the possibility that it functions in chromatin silencing in other eukaryotes.
claims.source: The conservation of all rixosome subunits from yeast to human raises the possibility that it functions in chromatin silencing in other eukaryotes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the conservation data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The rixosome may cleave nascent pol II-associated RNAs or mature chromatin associated RNAs in the path of nucleosome-bound Clr4.
claims.source: The rixosome may cleave nascent pol II-associated RNAs or mature chromatin associated RNAs in the path of nucleosome-bound Clr4.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the mechanism of rixosome function.

claims.claim: In the absence of the rixosome, the RNA pol II complex or chromatin-associated RNAs would create a barrier that blocks Clr4 read-write.
claims.source: In this model, in the absence of the rixosome, the RNA pol II complex or chromatin-associated RNAs would create a barrier that blocks Clr4 read-write (Figure 7B), which is required for both spreading of H3K9me from a nucleation point and its copying onto newly deposited nucleosomes following DNA replication.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the mechanism, illustrated in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The profound requirement for the rixosome in the spreading and epigenetic inheritance of H3K9me mirrors the requirement for the Clr4 read-write capability.
claims.source: In summary, the profound requirement for the rixosome in the spreading and epigenetic inheritance of H3K9me mirrors the requirement for the Clr4 read-write capability and supports the idea that the rixosome and read-write act coordinately during spreading and inheritance of H3K9me.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data showing similar phenotypes of rixosome and clr4 read-write mutants.

claims.claim: Subunits of the mammalian rixosome have been reported to interact with chromatin components.
claims.source: Finally, we note that subunits of the mammalian rixosome have been reported to interact with chromatin components and mutations in multiple subunits of the complex are associated with human disease (Fanis et al., 2012; Hussey et al., 2014; Sareddy and Vadlamudi, 2016).

claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The rixosome acts as a key trigger that promotes RNA degradation by the Dhp1/XRN2 exoribonuclease.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that heterochromatin-associated rixosome acts as a key trigger that promotes RNA degradation by the Dhp1/XRN2 exoribonuclease.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data on rixosome function and Dhp1 requirement.

claims.claim: The rixosome defines a second RNA degradation mechanism that localizes to heterochromatin and plays an indispensable role in heterochromatin spreading and maintenance in transcription units that are not associated with RNAi.
claims.source: The rixosome thus defines a second RNA degradation mechanism that localizes to heterochromatin, through direct recruitment by Swi6, and plays an indispensable role in heterochromatin spreading and maintenance in transcription units that are not associated with RNAi (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data showing rixosome function at the L(BglII):ade6+ transgene and its redundancy with RNAi at pericentromeric repeats.

claims.claim: During read-write, Clr4 binds to nucleosomes containing pre-existing H3K9me and catalyzes the methylation of histone H3 in adjacent nucleosomes.
claims.source: During read-write, Clr4 binds to nucleosomes containing pre-existing H3K9me and catalyzes the methylation of histone H3 in adjacent nucleosomes (Zhang et al., 2008; Al-Sady et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Fission yeast heterochromatic domains are associated with low levels of transcription and the synthesized RNA has been suggested to be retained by Swi6.
claims.source: Fission yeast heterochromatic domains are associated with low levels of transcription and the synthesized RNA has been suggested to be retained by Swi6 (Keller et al., 2012; Bühler et al., 2007; Kloc et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2008; Jih et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The crb3-D198N and grc3-G409E mutations show weak rRNA processing defects at elevated temperatures.
claims.source: We observed weak rRNA processing defects at elevated temperatures in cells carrying crb3-D198N and grc3-G409E mutations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by rRNA processing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The crb3-D198N mutation caused a 2-fold reduction in the levels of H3K9me3 at pericentromeric repeats in ago1+ cells.
claims.source: The crb3-D198N mutant caused a 2-fold reduction in the levels of H3K9me3, which may indicate a role for the rixosome in heterochromatin maturation (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: The Crb3-TAP purification from cells carrying the crb3-D198N mutation detected a modest reduction in the amount of co-precipitated Swi6.
claims.source: When we purified Crb3-TAP from cells carrying the crb3-D198N mutation, we detected a modest reduction in the amount of co-precipitated Swi6 in the mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which was not explained by a decrease in the overall Swi6 protein levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TMT-MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Other interactions, including those between the subunits of the rixosome complex, were weakly affected in the crb3-D198N mutant.
claims.source: However, other interactions, including those between the subunits of the rixosome complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 4), were also weakly affected, indicating that the stability of the complex in the crb3-D198 mutant may have been compromised.
claims.evidence: This is supported by TMT-MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The substitution of the central valine in the VxVxV motif with methionine would be expected to disrupt the binding surface for HP1 interaction.
claims.source: The substitution of the central valine in this motif, which is crucial for the interaction between HP1 and HP1-interacting proteins (Thiru et al., 2004), with methionine, would be expected to disrupt the binding surface.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of HP1-binding motifs, supported by citation.

claims.claim: In the crb3-D198N mutant, the localization of the rixosome was only modestly reduced.
claims.source: In the crb3-D198N mutant, which only partially reduced the association of the complex with the heterochromatic protein Swi6, the localization of the rixosome was only modestly reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The impairment of epigenetic maintenance in crb3-D198N mutant cells results from a rixosome defect downstream of its localization to heterochromatic domains.
claims.source: This result suggests that the impairment of epigenetic maintenance in crb3-D198N mutant cells results from a rixosome defect downstream of its localization to heterochromatic domains.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that localization is only modestly affected while maintenance is severely impaired.

claims.claim: The dis3-54 allele disrupted maintenance to a lesser extent than the dhp1-1 allele.
claims.source: Relative to the dhp1-1 allele, the dis3-54 allele disrupted maintenance to a lesser extent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silencing assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Deletion of cid14+ did not affect heterochromatin maintenance.
claims.source: Deletion of cid14+ did not affect heterochromatin maintenance and the cid14Δ grc3-V70M double mutant cells did not show any increase in gfp RNA relative to cid14Δ alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by silencing assay and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Under establishment conditions, the grc3-V70M mutant did not show an increase in gfp reporter RNA levels relative to wild-type cells.
claims.source: Under establishment condition, we did not observe an increase in gfp reporter RNA levels in the grc3-V70M mutant relative to wild-type cells.
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of RT-qPCR results.

claims.claim: Excess dg transcripts resulting from loss of rixosome-mediated degradation are rapidly processed into siRNAs by the RNAi pathway.
claims.source: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that excess dg transcripts, resulting from loss of rixosome-mediated degradation, are rapidly processed into siRNAs by the RNAi pathway (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased siRNAs but only modest increase in full-length transcripts.

claims.claim: The mutations in rixosome and dhp1 did not affect the levels of transcription from the pericentromeric dg repeats.
claims.source: Finally, RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) occupancy at the dg repeats was only weakly affected (Figure 5J), suggesting that the mutations did not affect the levels of transcription from the repeats.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from ChIP data shown in Figure 5J.

claims.claim: The read-write function of Clr4 is required for the transition from H3K9me2 to me3.
claims.source: Since the read-write function of Clr4 is required for the transition from H3K9me2 to me3 (Jih et al., 2017), these results raised the possibility that the rixosome-Dhp1 pathway was required for efficient Clr4 read-write.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Clr4 read-write is required for RNAi-independent spreading of H3K9me away from nucleation sites.
claims.source: In addition to efficient H3K9me3 deposition and epigenetic inheritance, Clr4 read-write is required for RNAi-independent spreading of H3K9me away from nucleation sites (Zhang et al., 2008; Jih et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In wild-type cells, heterochromatin spreads from the RNAi initiating centromere Homology (cenH) region into the mat2p gene and the adjacent IR-L boundary region.
claims.source: In wild-type cells, heterochromatin spreads from the RNAi initiating centromere Homology (cenH) region into the mat2p gene and the adjacent IR-L boundary region (Zhang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Transgenes inserted into the IR-L region display variable levels of silencing due to stochastic spreading of H3K9 methylation.
claims.source: Transgenes inserted into the IR-L region display variable levels of silencing due to stochastic spreading of H3K9 methylation and can therefore be used as a readout for heterochromatin spreading.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the IR-L reporter system.

claims.claim: The rixosome may perform a function analogous to that of the cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor (CPSF) complex at euchromatic mRNAs or the integrator complex.
claims.source: In the context of heterochromatin, the rixosome may perform a function that is analogous to that of the cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor (CPSF) complex at euchromatic mRNAs or the integrator complex which has been shown to release paused RNA pol II complexes (Shi and Manley, 2015, Elrod et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative comparison to other RNA processing complexes, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Unlike CPSF, which is recruited by specific polyadenylation signals in the 3' ends of mRNAs, the rixosome is recruited throughout heterochromatic domains via association with Swi6/HP1.
claims.source: However, unlike CPSF, which is recruited by specific polyadenylation signals in the 3' ends of mRNAs, the rixosome is recruited throughout heterochromatic domains via association with Swi6/HP1 and targets heterochromatic RNAs for degradation rather than polyadenylation and export.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on rixosome recruitment and function.

claims.claim: The role for the rixosome in heterochromatic RNA degradation is supported by the accumulation of heterochromatic RNAs in cells carrying rixosome mutations.
claims.source: The role for the rixosome in heterochromatic RNA degradation is supported by our demonstration that (1) heterochromatic RNAs accumulate in cells carrying rixosome mutations
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B, C and small RNA northern blot data in Figure 5G, H.

claims.claim: At pericentromeric DNA repeats where the RNAi machinery is recruited, the rixosome contributes to noncoding RNA degradation but is not required for H3K9me spreading, silencing, or inheritance unless the RNAi pathway is rendered inactive by mutation.
claims.source: For example, at pericentromeric DNA repeats where the RNAi machinery is recruited to nascent noncoding RNAs and processes them into siRNAs, the rixosome contributes to noncoding RNA degradation, but is not required for H3K9me spreading, silencing, or inheritance – unless the RNAi pathway is rendered inactive by mutation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data comparing ago1+ and ago1Δ cells (Figure 2F, G) and siRNA accumulation data (Figure 5G, H).

claims.claim: At the boundaries of the mating type locus, where no redundant RNA degradation pathway operates, rixosome-mediated RNA clearance is essential for heterochromatin spreading and silencing.
claims.source: By contrast, at the boundaries of the mating type locus, where no redundant RNA degradation pathway operates, rixosome-mediated RNA clearance is essential for heterochromatin spreading and silencing.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on the L(BglII):ade6+ transgene shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Both the spreading and epigenetic inheritance of heterochromatin require the read-write capability of the Clr4 methyltransferase.
claims.source: Both the spreading and epigenetic inheritance of heterochromatin require the read-write capability of the Clr4 methyltransferase (Zhang et al., 2008; Jih et al., 2017; Ragunathan et al., 2015; Audergon et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

results.result: The manuscript reviews established knowledge about heterochromatin formation and epigenetic inheritance, including the role of H3K9 methylation, read-write mechanisms, and DNA sequence-dependent and -independent pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C14 summarize well-established prior knowledge about heterochromatin biology in fission yeast, supported by appropriate citations to previous work. These provide necessary background context for the current study.

results.result: A genetic screen for epigenetic maintenance defective (emd) mutants identified mutations in 19 genes across five complexes, including four mutations in three rixosome subunits (crb3, grc3, mdn1).
results.evaluation: Claims C15, C20-C24 describe the genetic screen results with clear experimental data (Figure 1C, whole genome sequencing). The screening methodology is well-documented with appropriate controls and validation steps.

results.result: The rixosome is a conserved essential complex from yeast to humans containing six subunits with known roles in ribosomal RNA processing and previously shown to localize to heterochromatin.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C16-C18, C25-C26 accurately describe the rixosome complex based on prior literature (supported by citations) and data in Figure 2A showing conservation. This establishes the biological context for the novel findings.

results.result: The rixosome is required for epigenetic maintenance but not establishment of heterochromatin at both ectopic reporters and endogenous pericentromeric repeats.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C27-C32 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including silencing assays (Figure 2B), ChIP data for H3K9me2 under establishment and maintenance conditions (Figure 2D-G), and comparison of ago1+ vs ago1Δ backgrounds demonstrating maintenance-specific defects.

results.result: The grc3-V70M mutation is a separation-of-function allele that does not cause rRNA processing defects, while crb3-D198N and grc3-G409E show weak processing defects at elevated temperatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C33 and C85 are supported by rRNA processing data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) showing differential effects of mutations on ribosome biogenesis function. This validates grc3-V70M as suitable for studying heterochromatin-specific functions.

results.result: The grc3-V70M mutation specifically disrupts the rixosome's association with Swi6/HP1 without affecting complex integrity, while crb3-D198N shows modest effects on both Swi6 interaction and complex stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38, C87-C88 are supported by quantitative TMT-MS data (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and western blots (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E). The data clearly demonstrate selective loss of Swi6 interaction in grc3-V70M without affecting total Swi6 levels or overall complex integrity.

results.result: The grc3-V70M mutation is located in a VxVxV motif in the N-terminus of Grc3, a variant of the PxVxL HP1-binding motif, suggesting direct interaction between Grc3 and Swi6's chromoshadow domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40, C89 are supported by domain analysis (Figure 3D) and knowledge of HP1-binding motifs (cited from Thiru et al., 2004). The inference of direct interaction is reasonable given the mutation's location and the loss of Swi6 binding, though direct binding assays would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Crb3-TAP localizes to H3K9me2-containing heterochromatic domains in a Swi6-dependent manner, as the grc3-V70M mutation abolishes heterochromatin localization while preserving localization to tRNA gene clusters and other Swi6-independent sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C48, C90 are comprehensively supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data (Figure 3E-H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The data clearly show co-localization with H3K9me2 in wild-type and loss of heterochromatin localization in grc3-V70M, while maintaining localization to TFIIIC-recruited sites.

results.result: The crb3-D198N mutation impairs epigenetic maintenance through a defect downstream of rixosome localization to heterochromatin.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 is an inference based on modest reduction in localization (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) but severe maintenance defects. While plausible, the data showing only modest localization defects alongside compromised complex stability (C88) makes it difficult to definitively conclude the defect is purely downstream of localization.

results.result: The 5'→3' exonuclease Dhp1/XRN2, rather than the 3'→5' exosome, is the key RNA degradation pathway downstream of the rixosome required for heterochromatin maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51, C92 are supported by silencing assays and ChIP data (Figure 4A-B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing that dhp1-1 phenocopies rixosome mutants while dis3-54 has weaker effects. This establishes the 5'→3' pathway as the primary degradation mechanism.

results.result: The polynucleotide kinase activity of Grc3 is essential for epigenetic inheritance of heterochromatin, as catalytically dead Grc3 (K252A, S253A) fails to rescue the maintenance defect of grc3-G409E mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by rescue experiments (Figure 4C-D) showing that wild-type Grc3 restores maintenance while catalytically dead Grc3 does not. This directly demonstrates the requirement for kinase activity in preparing RNAs for Dhp1-mediated degradation.

results.result: Under establishment conditions, heterochromatic RNAs are targeted for degradation by both the rixosome and Ccr4-Not pathways, as revealed by RNA accumulation in caf1Δ grc3-V70M double mutants without corresponding increases in RNA Pol II occupancy.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57, C93-C94 are supported by RT-qPCR (Figure 5B-C) and ChIP data (Figure 5D-E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B) showing that deletion of caf1 unmasks the rixosome's role in RNA degradation. The lack of Pol II changes indicates post-transcriptional regulation.

results.result: At pericentromeric repeats, the rixosome competes with RNAi for RNA substrates, as rixosome and dhp1 mutations cause increased siRNA accumulation with only modest increases in full-length transcripts and no change in transcription levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63, C95-C96 are supported by small RNA northern blots (Figure 5G-H), RT-qPCR (Figure 5I), and Pol II ChIP (Figure 5J). The data showing increased siRNAs but modest transcript increases with unchanged Pol II occupancy strongly support the competition model between rixosome and RNAi pathways.

results.result: Rixosome and dhp1 mutations cause modest reductions in H3K9me3 levels at heterochromatic domains where the rixosome is enriched, suggesting a role in Clr4 read-write-mediated H3K9me3 deposition.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C86, C97 are supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D, Figure 2G) showing selective reduction of H3K9me3 at rixosome-enriched domains. The connection to Clr4 read-write is supported by citation to prior work showing read-write is required for me2→me3 transition.

results.result: The rixosome is essential for spreading of H3K9me and silencing across the transcriptionally active L(BglII):ade6+ transgene at the mating type locus, phenocopying clr4 read-write mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C73, C98-C100 are comprehensively supported by silencing assays (Figure 6B-D), RT-qPCR (Figure 6E), Pol II ChIP (Figure 6F), and H3K9me ChIP (Figure 6G-H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). The data clearly demonstrate that rixosome mutants block spreading into the transgene similarly to clr4-W31G, establishing the rixosome's essential role in heterochromatin spreading.

results.result: The rixosome is recruited to heterochromatin by Swi6/HP1 and targets heterochromatic RNAs for degradation through the 5'→3' exonuclease pathway, defining a second RNA degradation mechanism essential for heterochromatin spreading and maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C19, C63, C74, C81-C82, C102-C103 represent the main conclusions of the study, integrating multiple lines of evidence: Swi6 interaction (Figure 3), localization (Figure 3), RNA accumulation (Figure 5), kinase requirement (Figure 4), and Dhp1 dependence (Figure 4). The comprehensive data strongly support this model.

results.result: The rixosome functions redundantly with RNAi at pericentromeric repeats but is essential at the mating type locus boundaries where RNAi does not operate.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 are supported by comparing phenotypes at different genomic locations: pericentromeric repeats show defects only in ago1Δ background (Figure 2F-G) while the L(BglII):ade6+ transgene shows complete dependence on rixosome (Figure 6). This demonstrates context-dependent requirements for the rixosome.

results.result: The rixosome may cleave nascent or chromatin-associated RNAs to remove barriers that would otherwise block Clr4 read-write, analogous to CPSF or integrator complexes but recruited throughout heterochromatic domains via Swi6.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77, C101 present a mechanistic model that is plausible given the data but remains speculative. While the requirement for RNA degradation and read-write are established, direct evidence for RNA or Pol II acting as physical barriers to Clr4 is not provided. The model is reasonable but requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: The rixosome and Clr4 read-write act coordinately during spreading and inheritance of H3K9me, with both showing similar requirements for these processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C78, C83-C84, C108 are supported by the parallel phenotypes of rixosome and clr4-W31G mutants in spreading assays (Figure 6) and the established role of read-write in H3K9me propagation (supported by citations). The data showing similar defects in both mutants support coordinate action.

results.result: The conservation of rixosome subunits from yeast to humans, along with reported interactions with chromatin components and disease associations, suggests potential roles in chromatin silencing in other eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C75, C79-C80 are speculative regarding function in other organisms, though conservation is documented (Figure 2A) and prior work on mammalian rixosome is cited. The extrapolation to other eukaryotes is reasonable but requires experimental validation in those systems.
